subtopics.title: Meeting the Graph — Axes, Lines and the Story They Tell

questions.question: What should you always read FIRST on any graph?
options: The axes — their titles, units and scale
The steepest line
The intersection point
The colours of the lines

questions.question: Option B's line starts at R150 on the vertical axis. This intercept represents:
options: The price per unit
The fixed monthly charge paid even at zero usage
The break-even point
The maximum monthly cost

questions.question: Why does Option A's line start at the origin?
options: Because Option A has no fixed charge — zero usage costs zero rand
Because all graphs must start at zero
Because Option A is cheaper overall
Because the scale begins at zero

questions.question: In this tariff graph, the gradient of each line represents:
options: The fixed monthly charge
The price per kilowatt-hour — how much cost rises per extra unit
The total monthly bill
The number of appliances used

questions.question: Option A's line is steeper than Option B's because:
options: A charges R2,00 per unit while B charges only R1,50 per unit
A has a bigger fixed charge
A is drawn first
B has a bigger fixed charge

questions.question: On Option A's line the cost climbs from R200 at 100 kWh to R400 at 200 kWh. The gradient is:
options: R2,00 per kWh — a rise of R200 over 100 units
R200 per kWh
R0,50 per kWh
R4,00 per kWh

questions.question: The break-even point on this graph is at:
options: 300 kWh, where both options cost R600
150 kWh, where both options cost R300
450 kWh, where both options cost R825
0 kWh, where both options cost R150

questions.question: How is the break-even reading verified by calculation?
options: 300 × R2,00 = R600 for A, and R150 + 300 × R1,50 = R600 for B — both equal
R150 + R2,00 = R152 for both
600 ÷ 2 = 300 for both
It cannot be verified without the municipality's data

questions.question: For usage BELOW 300 kWh, which option is cheaper and why?
options: Option A — its line runs below B's, since light users avoid the R150 fixed charge
Option B — cheaper units always win
Both cost the same at all usages below 300
Option B — the fixed charge is refunded

questions.question: What does the break-even point mean for a decision-maker?
options: The usage at which both options cost the same — the point of indifference between them
The cheapest possible bill
The maximum usage allowed
The point where electricity becomes free

subtopics.title: Answering the 450 kWh Question — and the Exam Method

questions.question: At 450 kWh, the costs are:
options: A: R900; B: R825 — Option B is cheaper by R75
A: R825; B: R900 — Option A is cheaper by R75
Both cost R900

questions.question: Without calculating, how does zone logic answer the 450 kWh question?
options: 450 lies to the right of the 300 kWh break-even, and beyond break-even the fixed-charge option (B) is cheaper
450 is a big number, so the steeper line wins
The question cannot be answered without calculation
450 lies left of break-even, so A wins

questions.question: Why should a comparison answer state the rand difference, not just the winner?
options: Full marks for comparisons require showing both values and the saving (R75)
Because the difference changes the winner
It is optional decoration
To make the answer longer

questions.question: Which sense-check confirms the overall picture?
options: Heavy users benefiting from the fixed-charge option makes sense, since cheap units reward bulk usage
Electricity should always get cheaper as you use more
The lines should never cross on a real graph
Zero usage should cost the same on both options
